doc.title: Eddie Miller and Pete Fountain Interview, 1970-01-09

title: Doc Severinsen broadcast and local TV
summary: A caller asks whether Doc's visit would be broadcast; Pete cites union and record contracts and says local TV is too costly.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: That's very strange. Hello, go ahead. Hello? Turn your radio off, will you, sir?
All right. Go ahead. If you don't turn the radio off, we'll have difficulty, though.
I see. Yeah, I'd like to talk to Pete.
Yes, sir. Yep. Go ahead. Sir, turn the radio off, please.
Yeah, I'd like to ask if that show tonight, you say maybe Doc Severinsen might stop in. I'd like to know, would that be broadcast by any chance?

No, we're not going to tape it or anything. We couldn't anyway, unless we had permission through the union. And he records for command records, and I record for Decker, so we couldn't... All those people there, then, huh? Well, with the company, it's not between he and I. He and I have been good buddies for the last, I'd say, eight years.

Uh-huh. And I was wondering, too, Pete, how come, in other words, like you and Al Hurt, how come they don't give, well, have, say, somewhat like a television program here local with such great talent as you and Al?

Well, they were trying to get something like that going here, but it just wouldn't work out. I guess it's too expensive to come down here and do it. I see. It's cheaper to fly us up there to New York or California, or, like I said, Nashville's doing a lot of work. I'll be doing a lot of TV out of there soon. I see.
Okay, Pete, enjoy talking. Thank you.
Thank you. Bye. Bye. 522-3791. We have about five minutes left. And Eddie Miller and Pete Fountner with us tonight. Hello. Go ahead, please.
